claims.claim: Wolfe plants each clue exactly once and refuses to repeat it, on the principle that a clue told five times is written for someone dumber than the reader.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview (Shadows of the New Sun)
claims.quote: I try not to leave a clue more than once

claims.claim: He says he leaves all the clues a reader will need and often more, because in real detection the work is finding more clues, not reasoning harder from a few.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: very little of it consists of reasoning from clues

claims.claim: Wolfe denies writing perspectival novels where confusion is the point: the clues are there, the puzzles are meant to be solved, and superficial confusion is simply how life looks before you think about it.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: Life seen superficially has very little pattern to it.

claims.feature: style suited to the story; journalistic third person
claims.claim: He writes each book in the style its story calls for; the third-person Long Sun therefore came out as plain, journalistic prose rather than the stylized first-person of the Severian books.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: pretty much straightforward journalistic prose

claims.claim: In Castleview different characters see the same unexplained thing as cowboys, Arthurian knights or a spaceship, modelled on anomaly reports where two witnesses describe a third thing differently.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: two witnesses who have very different stories

claims.feature: supernatural premise to license memory's vividness
claims.claim: Wolfe made Weer a dead man rather than a reminiscing old man so the remembered rooms could be re-created with a strength ordinary reminiscence could not justify.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: lend to the memories certain supernatural strengths

claims.feature: ghost making sense of his life
claims.claim: He conceived Peace not as purgatory but as a ghost trying to make sense of his own life, and accepts purgatory as another way of saying the same thing.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: a ghost trying to make sense of his own life

claims.claim: The Soldier books are built to show the problems of a genuinely good man who cannot remember, which Wolfe maps onto a decent society that has no awareness of its history.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: a genuinely good man who can't remember

claims.feature: writing the pagan world from inside its belief
claims.claim: For the Soldier books he wrote the ancient world as the pagans wrote about it rather than through the rationalist modern historian, so gods appear as the characters expected them to.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: as the pagans themselves wrote about it

claims.claim: Wolfe says he used the memory-palace system of Simonides in the Soldier books.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: made use of the memory palace system

claims.claim: He says symbolic details arrive as local impulses ('that's neat; I'll do that') and denies the books are allegories.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: The book isn't intended as an allegory.

claims.claim: Wolfe claims he can identify a writer from a paragraph or two and could write imitation Shakespeare or Lewis that passes, a self-described knack for voice.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: I am a good imitator.

claims.claim: He describes the Severian books as in part his decision to rewrite The Dying Earth from his own standpoint, openly acknowledging Vance and Clark Ashton Smith.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: rewrite The Dying Earth from my own standpoint

claims.claim: Asked whether he invented any words, Wolfe answers that some odd words in the New Sun are typos, warning readers against treating every oddity as a clue.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: some of them are typos

claims.claim: He reads scriptural images (the apple, the sky rolled up) as figurative language giving a general idea to an audience unable to grasp the actuality, a model for conveying meaning in pictures.
claims.source: Jordan 1992 interview
claims.quote: figurative language to try to give a general idea

claims.claim: Any narrator who is a person inside the story is going to be unreliable; five or six honest courtroom witnesses to one event all report different things.
claims.source: Person 1998 (Nova Express) interview
claims.quote: the narrator is damn well going to be unreliable

claims.feature: unattributed dialogue by idiolect and content
claims.claim: Speakers in crowded Long Sun scenes are identified without tags by characteristic phrases or mistakes and by each saying only what that character would say in that circumstance.
claims.source: Person 1998 interview
claims.quote: saying something that only Maytera Marble would say

claims.claim: The more complex the story, the clearer its narrative structure must be; shaken up, a ten-thousand-part machine is just a box of junk.
claims.source: Person 1998 interview
claims.quote: it isn't complex, it's simply confused

claims.claim: For the New Sun he refused Tars-Tarkas-style invented names and used archaic names and terms in contexts where the reader can work out what is meant.
claims.source: Person 1998 interview
claims.quote: not coining Tars Tarkas type names

claims.claim: He finds the Latin or Greek word for the thing he needs, then searches unabridged dictionaries on the assumption that someone once anglicised it, often finding an 18th-century citation.
claims.source: Person 1998 interview
claims.quote: someone will have anglicised this term

claims.claim: In Fifth Head the story attributed to John V. Marsch is actually written by the shadowchild who replaced him, a trick Wolfe concedes is New Wave.
claims.source: Person 1998 interview
claims.quote: not actually written by John V. Marsch

claims.feature: diversity of registers within one world
claims.claim: Wolfe rejects monocultured SF worlds as mental sloth, noting that in one big city people at different social levels already speak almost different languages.
claims.source: Person 1998 interview
claims.quote: Mental sloth more than anything else.

claims.feature: revision turns synopsis into hard facts
claims.claim: Wolfe often first writes synopsis and in revision lengthens it, turning generalities into hard facts and making each speaker talk as she talks.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2008 (Jones)
claims.quote: I turned generalities into hard facts.

claims.claim: He forbids himself sentences like 'Nick was a bad man and a cruel man' and must instead show Nick being bad within the story.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2008 (Jones)
claims.quote: Easy writing makes damned hard reading.

claims.claim: He stops when he can no longer tell whether changes improve the piece, usually after four drafts; a fifth that reverts to the second is a bad sign.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2008 (Jones)
claims.quote: A fifth draft may find me reverting

claims.claim: Dialogue must entertain, forward the plot and characterize the speaker at once, and sound like what that speaker would say to that person then.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2008 (Jones)
claims.quote: Dialogue is action.

claims.claim: Even unimportant characters must speak differently from one another; students reject this because everybody sounds alike to them.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2008 (Jones)
claims.quote: The butler mustn't sound like the footman

claims.claim: Like poetry and song, fiction demands the concrete; he contrasts an abstract shipwreck summary with a ballad naming the ship, the cargo and the shoal.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2008 (Jones)
claims.quote: fiction demands the concrete

claims.feature: expectation and satisfaction as story engine
claims.claim: A short story works by engendering expectations and satisfying them; he told a student to post a sign reading 'I AM GOING TO TELL YOU SOMETHING COOL'.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2008 (Jones)
claims.quote: engendering expectations and satisfying them

claims.claim: Realistic fiction leaves out far too much of human experience; fantasy is nearer the truth.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2008 (Jones)
claims.quote: Realistic fiction leaves out far, far too much.

claims.claim: Style should suit the story; a wrong style is comic for ten pages, and the narrator's voice is inseparable from style.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2008 (Jones)
claims.quote: the style should suit the story

claims.feature: narrator may comment; author may not
claims.claim: First person puts the reader inside the story and lets the narrator comment on actions, whereas authorial comment is usually ruinously bad.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2015 (Baker)
claims.quote: it's usually ruinously bad

claims.claim: Narrators are either openly unreliable or pretend to be totally reliable, but all are unreliable because people write books and people cannot be trusted.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2015 (Baker)
claims.quote: narrators that pretend to be totally reliable

claims.feature: reader sees self in the text
claims.claim: Off-the-wall interpretations no longer surprise him because readers look into the story and see themselves.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2015 (Baker)
claims.quote: what they are seeing is themselves

claims.claim: Fictional villains have narrow viewpoints; a real villain never thinks he is a villain, which shapes how bad men narrate themselves.
claims.source: Clarkesworld 2015 (Baker)
claims.quote: a real villain never thinks he's a villain

claims.claim: Characterization is done only by showing the character thinking, speaking and acting characteristically, never by telling the reader about him.
claims.source: Black Gate 2010 (Cooney)
claims.quote: You simply show it and shut up.

claims.claim: Do not start a story without an ending in mind; the ending may change but there must always be a destination.
claims.source: Black Gate 2010 (Cooney)
claims.quote: you should always have a destination

claims.claim: He does almost no research before writing and fills in world details as he reaches them, researching as he goes (what Greeks ate for breakfast: nothing).
claims.source: Black Gate 2010 (Cooney)
claims.quote: I do research while I'm writing the book.

claims.claim: In 'The Tree Is My Hat' the ex-wife's name Mary Christmas is never stated; the reader finds it out by deduction.
claims.source: Black Gate 2010 (Cooney)
claims.quote: you find out by deduction

claims.claim: Severian began as a costume (boots, trousers, no shirt, cloak, mask, sword) from which Wolfe deduced the man, an executioner.
claims.source: Black Gate 2010 (Cooney)
claims.quote: He's an executioner.

claims.claim: Wolfe says the storytelling contest in the third New Sun volume is strictly padding added when the publisher split the book.
claims.source: Black Gate 2010 (Cooney)
claims.quote: a storytelling contest that's strictly padding

claims.claim: Wolfe attributes the shorter paragraphs and looser tone of his later books to criticism for being unreadable and overcomplex, after which he decided to loosen up.
claims.source: MIT Technology Review 2014
claims.quote: criticism for being unreadable and overcomplex

claims.feature: difficulty as duty to the reader
claims.claim: He sets himself hard technical challenges with narrators because an author who makes everything easy for himself bores the reader.
claims.source: MIT Technology Review 2014
claims.quote: you bore the reader

claims.feature: ghost who does not know he is dead
claims.claim: Weer's unreliability is that he is a ghost, and ghosts often do not realize they are dead.
claims.source: MIT Technology Review 2014
claims.quote: Ghosts often don't realize they're dead.

claims.feature: narrator talking himself into a false identity
claims.claim: Marsch in Fifth Head knows he is not a real Earthman but is trying to talk himself into believing he is.
claims.source: MIT Technology Review 2014
claims.quote: trying to talk himself into believing that he is

claims.claim: A naive observer is more interesting because he gives only what he has seen, whereas adult witnesses cannot separate what they saw from what it means.
claims.source: MIT Technology Review 2014
claims.quote: he's just giving you what he has seen

claims.feature: perfect memory and daily amnesia as inverse designs
claims.claim: Having built Severian to forget nothing, Wolfe built Latro from a real brain injury to forget everything.
claims.source: MIT Technology Review 2014
claims.quote: let's do one of these guys who forgets everything

claims.claim: Every narrator is unreliable because each sees from his own standpoint and not another's.
claims.source: MIT Technology Review 2014
claims.quote: They're all unreliable. Well, we all are, aren't we?

claims.feature: epistolary entry with per-writer style shifts
claims.claim: He recommends The Sorcerer's House as an entry point because the epistolary form helps readers, provided they accept the style changing with each letter writer.
claims.source: MIT Technology Review 2014
claims.quote: the style changes from one letter writer to another

claims.claim: Military service teaches you to look at scenery as defensive positions, the perception behind Severian's line that war is a new geography.
claims.source: MIT Technology Review 2014
claims.quote: look at scenery from a standpoint of defensive positions

claims.claim: Wolfe learned prose from a college editor who blue-pencilled every word a sentence did not require, and he wrote the next story so it could not be cut.
claims.source: Locus Sept 2002 (Gaiman/Wolfe)
claims.quote: taking out every word the sentence

claims.claim: His definition of good literature is what an educated reader can read and reread with increased pleasure, and he refuses to write fiction that gives everything up on first reading.
claims.source: Locus Sept 2002 (Gaiman/Wolfe)
claims.quote: reread with increased pleasure

claims.claim: He will not adjudicate readers' theories about the text because he argues from presumed expertise on an unlevel field, and there is no sacredness to the text.
claims.source: Locus Sept 2002 (Gaiman/Wolfe)
claims.quote: no sacredness to the text

claims.claim: Wolfe says readers will see things in the books he does not see consciously, and that he likes those things.
claims.source: Locus Sept 2002 (Gaiman/Wolfe)
claims.quote: I like those things.

claims.feature: Peace built on lies (Gaiman) vs. 'I never lie'
claims.claim: Gaiman calls Wolfe the master of lying in fiction and says Peace is built on lies decipherable after three or four readings; Wolfe replies that he never lies.
claims.source: Locus Sept 2002 (Gaiman/Wolfe)
claims.quote: I never lie.

claims.feature: fiction as assurance that things need not be as they are
claims.claim: The most important thing fiction does is assure the reader that things need not be as they are now, which Wolfe names hope.
claims.source: Locus Sept 2002 (Gaiman/Wolfe)
claims.quote: the most important thing is hope

claims.claim: Anything in a book must do several things at once (tone, plot, character); a 'pass the salt' line is waste unless said in a particular way or for a purpose.
claims.source: Locus March 2011 excerpts
claims.quote: you really have to be doing several things at once

claims.claim: Wolfe denies his style has changed at all: he writes in a voice appropriate to the story he has to tell.
claims.source: SF Site Jan 2002 (Gevers)
claims.quote: I write in a voice appropriate to the story

claims.claim: A style becomes difficult only when it is not suited to what is being said; if it is the right style he likes it, if not he changes it.
claims.source: SF Site Jan 2002 (Gevers)
claims.quote: A style becomes difficult when it is not suited

claims.claim: Character speech comes from listening to what people actually say as well as what they mean; Remora and Incus are slight exaggerations of real people, and Oreb manages only two syllables.
claims.source: SF Site Jan 2002 (Gevers)
claims.quote: what they actually say as well as what they mean

claims.claim: For about half the first draft of Long Sun Wolfe did not know who was writing it, considered Maytera Marble, settled on Horn and rewrote accordingly.
claims.source: SF Site Jan 2002 (Gevers)
claims.quote: I didn't know who was writing

claims.feature: third person would be dead on the page
claims.claim: He chose Short Sun's interwoven narrators because telling it in third person would have been dead on the page; the difficulty was balancing storylines.
claims.source: SF Site Jan 2002 (Gevers)
claims.quote: it would have been dead there on the page

claims.feature: secondary narrators reconstruct honestly but fallibly
claims.claim: Daisy, principal writer of the Whorl chapters, strings others' accounts into plausible incidents and has deliberately falsified nothing, leaving errors to ignorance not intent.
claims.source: SF Site Jan 2002 (Gevers)
claims.quote: She has deliberately falsified nothing.

claims.claim: Asked directly whether Pig is a godling, Wolfe says certainly, since there are telltale signs all through the book.
claims.source: SF Site Jan 2002 (Gevers)
claims.quote: There are telltale signs all through the book.

claims.feature: the reader is expected to get it
claims.claim: He is surprised readers missed the inhumi secret (they prey on us because we prey on each other), which he thought everyone would get.
claims.source: SF Site Jan 2002 (Gevers)
claims.quote: I thought that everyone would get it

claims.claim: Wolfe cites Roger Rabbit slipping the handcuffs 'only when it's funny' as the law binding writers: a gun on the wall in Act I must be fired.
claims.source: SF Site Jan 2002 (Gevers)
claims.quote: No, only when it's funny.

claims.feature: story built backward from an ending image
claims.claim: He constructs a clued short story from one or more ideas and an ending image, answering the questions that image raises before writing.
claims.source: SF Site Jan 2002 (Gevers)
claims.quote: I have one or more ideas, and an ending

claims.claim: Gevers characterizes Wolfe's range as writing alternately with limpid simplicity and formidable baroque density of diction, in the service of oblique many-layered fictions.
claims.source: SF Site Jan 2002 (Gevers, introduction)
claims.quote: a formidable baroque density of diction

claims.claim: Ambiguity is necessary in some of his stories and not in others; where present it contributes richness, but he doubts thematic closure is never attainable.
claims.source: Infinity Plus 2003
claims.quote: Ambiguity is necessary in some of my stories, not in all.

claims.claim: The Knight's narrator is a contemporary American because Wolfe needed someone from outside who would not have grown up hearing of the Aelf and Angrborn.
claims.source: Infinity Plus 2003
claims.quote: who would not have heard about the Aelf

claims.claim: Asked how he came to write dimly-seen higher powers behind human events, Wolfe answers only 'No comment', leaving discovery to the reader.
claims.source: Infinity Plus 2003
claims.quote: No comment.

claims.feature: do not dumb down pivotal events
claims.claim: Wolfe holds that people's pivotal life events as they actually occurred would not be believed, and that literature should not dumb reality down but smart it up.
claims.source: Baber 1994 interview
claims.quote: we don't dumb it down

claims.claim: Real complex character comes from people who are rotten only selectively, nice to their drinking buddies, unlike utopian or dystopian casts.
claims.source: Baber 1994 interview
claims.quote: most rotten people are only rotten selectively

claims.feature: paper is paper: the concrete credo
claims.claim: Against a materialist correspondent Wolfe insists a piece of paper is a piece of paper and cheese is cheese, the animal-level knowing that living and, by implication, fiction require.
claims.source: Baber 1994 interview
claims.quote: It is paper. It is cheese.

claims.feature: write a book, not a genre
claims.claim: He defends mixing private eyes and witches in one SF novel because such people exist; he is not trying to write genres.
claims.source: Baber 1994 interview
claims.quote: I'm not trying to write genres

claims.claim: Asked why he is drawn to deceptions that turn out to be true, Wolfe says it must be the unconscious hope that some of his will.
claims.source: Cloud Chamber 77 (1997)
claims.quote: the unconscious hope that some of mine will

claims.claim: Scenes Horn could not have witnessed are sourced within the fiction (an unnamed kite builder; prayers written by Horn and Nettle who heard Silk pray), and Wolfe points to a page in Exodus.
claims.source: Cloud Chamber 77 (1997)
claims.quote: Please reread Exodus, p. 371.

claims.feature: happened / probably happened / must have happened
claims.claim: Horn and Nettle tell what happened, what probably happened and what must have happened, in dramatic form; their account is necessarily subjective and they make mistakes.
claims.source: Cloud Chamber 77 (1997)
claims.quote: what probably happened, and what must have happened

claims.claim: Wolfe concedes the Mint/Marble location swap in Exodus is his mistake; Langford notes readers had been reading subtleties into his least typos.
claims.source: Cloud Chamber 77 (1997)
claims.quote: they are my mistakes

claims.feature: literal answer to a symbolic question
claims.claim: Asked who or what Oreb is, Wolfe answers only that Oreb is a night chough, declining the symbolic reading the questioner wanted.
claims.source: Cloud Chamber 77 (1997)
claims.quote: Oreb is a night chough.

claims.feature: answers deferred to the next book
claims.claim: Some questions (Quetzal's motive) are answered only by telling the reader to read the next series, keeping the withholding in force.
claims.source: Cloud Chamber 77 (1997)
claims.quote: You will have to read The Book

claims.claim: Wolfe reads Tolkien as having uncovered a forgotten Folk Law and built Middle-earth as a means of displaying it in the clearest light, planting the truth that society need not be as we see it.
claims.source: The Best Introduction to the Mountains (2001)
claims.quote: society need not be as we see it around us

claims.claim: He describes rationing The Fellowship to one chapter an evening while permitting himself to reread earlier chapters endlessly, the habit of the rereader he later writes for.
claims.source: The Best Introduction to the Mountains (2001)
claims.quote: no more than a single chapter each evening

claims.feature: etymology inside and outside the story
claims.claim: Tolkien's reply to Wolfe's fan letter distinguishes a word's etymology within the story from the author's source for it, a distinction Wolfe's own Latinate diction depends on.
claims.source: The Best Introduction to the Mountains (2001)
claims.quote: two sides

claims.feature: trust the text / do not trust the text
claims.claim: Gaiman's first two rules: trust the text implicitly because the answers are in there, and do not trust it farther than you can throw it because it may go off in your hand.
claims.source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
claims.quote: Trust the text implicitly. The answers are in there.

claims.claim: The books subtly reshape themselves while you are away; Peace was a gentle Midwestern memoir on first reading and a horror novel on the second or third.
claims.source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
claims.quote: It only became a horror novel on the second

claims.claim: Wolfe is the kind of clever writer who sees no need to point out his cleverness; the intelligence serves the tale and makes the reader smart too.
claims.source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
claims.quote: He is smart to make you smart as well.

claims.claim: Rule 8 asserts the author was there and knows whose reflection they saw in the mirror, i.e. the withheld fact is known and recoverable.
claims.source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe
claims.quote: He knows whose reflection they saw in the mirror

claims.claim: Gaiman reports Wolfe solving a ninety-year-old murder from a press clipping (the matches by the railway tracks), evidence of the engineer's mind behind the clue-planting.
claims.source: Gaiman, How to Read Gene Wolfe / journal
claims.quote: He has an engineer's mind

claims.feature: story knows more than it says
claims.claim: Clute's summary law: a Wolfe story always knows more than it says and can almost never be fully grasped on a first reading.
claims.source: Clute, SFE entry
claims.quote: A Wolfe story always knows more than it says

claims.claim: The true story is conveyed by indirection and reveals itself through the reader's ultimate decipherment.
claims.source: Clute, SFE entry
claims.quote: conveyed by indirection

claims.claim: Fifth Head's clues are almost subliminal on first pass but in retrospect or after rereading lucid and inevitable, and the key twists are extractable from the manuscript that tells the story.
claims.source: Clute, SFE entry
claims.quote: in retrospect or after rereading almost invariably lucid

claims.claim: Clute names the structure shared by the major works 'recursive retrospect': a narrator looking back on events whose meaning loops back on the telling.
claims.source: Clute, SFE entry
claims.quote: recursive retrospect

claims.claim: Wolfe's reticences of presentation make the work very nearly opaque, combining the utterly present and the implacably remote.
claims.source: Clute, SFE entry
claims.quote: taxing reticences of presentation

claims.claim: Peace is a childhood narrated all unknowingly from beyond the grave, its truth value unrelentingly put under the question.
claims.source: Clute, SFE entry
claims.quote: unrelentingly put under the question

claims.feature: sins of omission with visible gaps
claims.claim: Severian's unreliability is mostly omission; the gaps are not hidden but catch gently on first reading and insistently on rereading.
claims.source: Evenson, Reactor 2021
claims.quote: more sins of omission than outright deception

claims.feature: telling order differs from event order
claims.claim: The rearranged order of recounting, combined with gaps, leaves it uncertain whether Severian hides things or merely tells what he wants in the order he wants, making the unreliability feel human rather than literary.
claims.source: Evenson, Reactor 2021
claims.quote: less literarily motivated, more informal and human

claims.claim: Severian's obscure wish to carry the moon-landing picture to a forest reads as random until pages later we learn the moon is now forested; Wolfe often passes such moments in silence.
claims.source: Evenson, Reactor 2021
claims.quote: we later discover that it's exactly right

claims.claim: After absorbing Thecla and the Autarch the narrator is a multiplicity speaking as a oneness; a parenthetical memory of torturing for fun turns out to be Thecla's.
claims.source: Evenson, Reactor 2021
claims.quote: a multiplicity trying to speak as if it were a oneness

claims.feature: chapter ends in muddle explained next chapter (reader comment)
claims.claim: A commenter observes that chapters tend to end in an incoherent hugger-mugger that the next chapter's opening explains.
claims.source: Evenson, Reactor 2021 (comment by NancyLebovitz)
claims.quote: explained at the beginning of the next chapter

claims.feature: miracle never acknowledged by the narrator (reader comment)
claims.claim: Commenters note Severian resurrects Dorcas with the Claw and never states that he did so, even after he learns the Claw's power.
claims.source: Evenson, Reactor 2021 (comments by AndyLove, pfsmith)

claims.claim: Wolfe eschews neologism; his obscure real words work at a surface level, a mystery-clue level and an allusive level, which drives close reading and rereading.
claims.source: Gerwel 2014
claims.quote: Wolfe eschews the use of neologism

claims.claim: Peace never states that its narrator is dead, in a memory-palace purgatory, and probably a multiple murderer; the reader must identify and solve the puzzle from clues.
claims.source: Gerwel 2014
claims.quote: a puzzle which must be identified and then solved

claims.feature: first sentence paid off by one later line
claims.claim: The opening sentence about the fallen elm becomes clear only when connected to a single, seemingly unrelated line of dialogue in the novel's final third.
claims.source: Gerwel 2014
claims.quote: a different, single, and seemingly unrelated line

claims.claim: Severian cannot forget yet lies and is inconsistent; Latro cannot remember yet his narrative is consistent, an inversion that asks which narrator is trustworthy.
claims.source: Gerwel 2014
claims.quote: his narrative is consistent throughout

claims.claim: The Latro books frame the scrolls through a translator who notes the narrator's limited ability to write and the haste of composition, layering unreliability.
claims.source: Gerwel 2014
claims.quote: limited ability to write

claims.claim: Wolfe's density comes from what he leaves out rather than elaborate description; suggestion through omission gives the prose its depth.
claims.source: Ewing 2010
claims.quote: what Wolfe's leaves out that gives it its depth

claims.claim: The sentences are clear, cut back and almost Hemingwayesque, while exotic nouns like 'burginot' estrange without obscuring.
claims.source: Ewing 2010
claims.quote: cut back and simplified, almost Hemmingwayesque

claims.claim: Wolfe's narrators often know little, placing them in the reader's position; 'Tracking Song' opens by telling its narrator he knows nothing.
claims.source: Ewing 2010
claims.quote: You know nothing.

claims.feature: unexplained detail implies a larger world
claims.claim: Wolfe takes Heinlein's 'the door dilated' further, using unexplained background details to imply worlds, and leaves questions half-answered as a feature.
claims.source: Ewing 2010
claims.quote: takes this to the next level

claims.claim: Peter Wright's Attending Daedalus casts Wolfe as encoder and the reader as decoder of labyrinthine conundrums, with the element of choice as his principal device for confounding the reader.
claims.source: LARB 2013 (quoting Wright)
claims.quote: Wolfe's principal device for confounding the reader

claims.claim: Wright records that no reviewer recognised Weer's deathly state, making Peace Wolfe's first misinterpreted narrative.
claims.source: LARB 2013 (quoting Wright)
claims.quote: Wolfe's first misinterpreted narrative

claims.claim: The reviewer maintains the novel contains as many readings as readers and resists the reading that Wolfe aims to confound.
claims.source: LARB 2013
claims.quote: as many readings perhaps as there are readers

claims.feature: cascading metaphor in the cosmic register
claims.claim: Peace's first section collapses SF's cosmic perspective into religious ecstasy and cascades from metaphor to metaphor; no one else writes like that.
claims.source: LARB 2013
claims.quote: cascading from metaphor to metaphor

claims.feature: author claims kinship with his ghost
claims.claim: Wolfe is quoted as saying of Weer that they have similar souls, against readings of Weer as the devil.
claims.source: LARB 2013 (Wolfe quoted)
claims.quote: we have similar souls

claims.claim: Weer leaves stories unfinished and declines to narrate the visit to Gold's farm, later revealing he murdered the librarian; the reader must sift the evidence.
claims.source: Jacobs 2024
claims.quote: the reader has to sift the evidence

claims.feature: interpolated tales comment on the frame
claims.claim: The embedded tales comment in various ways on the events Weer narrates, and the reader must decide which ones do.
claims.source: Jacobs 2024
claims.quote: comment in various ways on the events

claims.claim: Weer lives in a rambling memory palace of his own making whose rooms he can temporarily or permanently lose access to.
claims.source: Jacobs 2024
claims.quote: a rambling memory palace of his own making

claims.feature: lie in dialogue, not in narration
claims.claim: Wolfe's characters will lie in dialogue but not in narration, so narrative statements can be trusted while speech cannot.
claims.source: The Solute 2017
claims.quote: characters will lie in dialogue but not in narration

claims.feature: narration stops just before a death
claims.claim: Weer's narration stops just before a character dies and resumes later, so murders are inferred from absence, a 'shadow narrative'.
claims.source: The Solute 2017
claims.quote: stops just before a character dies

claims.claim: The Boy Scout knife that Weer can never locate, and the pun in 'my den, where I now never go', carry double meanings the narrator does not acknowledge.
claims.source: The Solute 2017
claims.quote: my den, where I now never go

claims.claim: The layered tales let Weer escape: as long as he keeps telling stories he need not face what comes next.
claims.source: The Solute 2017
